cards.title: A crystal whose light speed depends on direction
cards.meaning: An anisotropic crystal is one whose refractive index changes with the direction of light travel.
points: Glass, water, air: same index in every direction (isotropic).
Crystal: atoms are arranged differently along different directions.
Uniaxial (calcite, quartz, tourmaline): one ordinary and one extraordinary ray.
Biaxial (mica, topaz, aragonite): both refracted rays are extraordinary.

cards.label: 01 · §20.10 Definition
cards.title: What is an anisotropic crystal?
cards.body: An anisotropic crystal is one in which the refractive index depends on the direction of light travel.
points: Isotropic media such as glass, water and air have one index in all directions.
Atom arrangement differs with direction, so the light speed differs too.
Uniaxial crystals: calcite, quartz, tourmaline. Biaxial: mica, topaz, aragonite.

cards.title: One ray entering, two rays leaving
cards.meaning: Double refraction is the splitting of one incident ray into two refracted rays inside an anisotropic crystal.
points: Calcite (Iceland spar): colourless and transparent; it splits a ray in two.
Test: a mark seen through calcite shows two images.
Rotate the crystal about the o-image: the e-image moves in a circle.

cards.label: 02 · §20.11 Definition
cards.title: What is double refraction?
cards.body: Double refraction is the splitting of an incident ray into an ordinary and an extraordinary ray inside a crystal.
points: Calcite (Iceland spar) is the standard example; it is a negative crystal.
The o-ray obeys the laws of refraction; the e-ray does not.
Birefringence is the difference of the two indices (Eq. 20.11).

cards.title: The one direction with no double refraction
cards.meaning: The optic axis is a crystal direction along which light is not split into two rays.
points: Direction, not a line: any line parallel to it is also an optic axis.
Speed: the o-ray and e-ray travel with the same speed along it.
Symmetry: the crystal structure is symmetric about this direction.

cards.label: 03 · §20.10.2 Definition
cards.title: What is the optic axis?
cards.body: The optic axis is the direction in a uniaxial crystal along which the o-ray and e-ray travel with the same speed.
points: It bisects a blunt corner (A or H) at equal angles to the three edges there.
Joining the two blunt corners gives its direction only if the three edges are equal.
Light along it is not doubly refracted.
Its refractive index is the ordinary index \(\mu_o\).

objects.text: o and e: same speed here
objects.name: cap

cards.title: A slice through the crystal that holds the optic axis
cards.meaning: A principal section is a plane containing the optic axis, perpendicular to a pair of opposite faces.
points: Three principal sections pass through any point: one per pair of opposite faces.
Calcite: its principal section is a parallelogram with angles 71° and 109°.
Vibrations: the e-ray is parallel to it; the o-ray is perpendicular to it.

cards.label: 04 · §20.10.3 Definition
cards.title: What is a principal section?
cards.body: A principal section is the plane that contains the optic axis and is perpendicular to a pair of opposite crystal faces.
points: Through any point there are three, one for each pair of opposite faces.
In calcite it cuts the crystal in a parallelogram with angles 71° and 109°.
If the plane of incidence is a principal section, the e-ray stays in that plane.

cards.title: Each ray has its own plane through the optic axis
cards.meaning: A principal plane contains the optic axis and one refracted ray, either the o-ray or the e-ray.
points: Two planes: one for the o-ray and one for the e-ray.
Usually the two principal planes do not coincide.
Use: they fix the vibration direction of each ray.

cards.label: 05 · §20.10.4 Definition
cards.title: What is a principal plane?
cards.body: A principal plane is the plane that contains the optic axis and one of the two refracted rays, the o-ray or the e-ray.
points: There is a principal plane of the o-ray and a separate one of the e-ray.
In general the two principal planes do not coincide.
When the plane of incidence is a principal section, all three planes coincide.

cards.title: The ray with the same speed in every direction
cards.meaning: The ordinary (o) ray is the refracted ray that obeys the ordinary laws of refraction.
points: Speed: \(v_o\) is the same in every direction inside the crystal.
Index: \(\mu_o\) is a constant.
Plane: it always lies in the plane of incidence.

cards.label: 06 · §20.11.2 Definition
cards.title: What is the ordinary ray?
cards.body: The ordinary (o) ray is the refracted ray in an anisotropic crystal that obeys the ordinary laws of refraction.
points: Its wave surface is a sphere, since its speed is the same in all directions.
It always lies in the plane of incidence.
Linearly polarised, vibrating perpendicular to its principal section.

cards.title: The ray whose speed changes with direction
cards.meaning: The extraordinary (e) ray is the refracted ray that does not obey the ordinary laws of refraction.
points: Speed: depends on the direction of travel inside the crystal.
Index: \(\mu_e\) varies with direction.
Plane: it leaves the plane of incidence unless that plane is a principal section.

cards.label: 07 · §20.11.2 Definition
cards.title: What is the extraordinary ray?
cards.body: The extraordinary (e) ray is the refracted ray in an anisotropic crystal whose speed and refractive index depend on its direction.
points: Its wave surface is an ellipsoid of revolution about the optic axis.
Linearly polarised, vibrating parallel to its principal section.
The o and e labels have meaning only inside the crystal.

cards.title: Which wave surface sits inside the other
cards.meaning: Positive and negative crystals differ in whether the e-wave surface lies inside or outside the o-wave sphere.
points: Negative (calcite): the o-sphere lies inside the e-ellipsoid.
Positive (quartz): the e-ellipsoid lies inside the o-sphere.
Index: negative means \(\mu_e < \mu_o\); positive means \(\mu_e > \mu_o\).

cards.label: 08 · §20.11.3 Definition
cards.title: What is a negative crystal?
cards.body: A negative crystal is a uniaxial crystal in which the e-ray index is less than the o-ray index, \(\mu_e < \mu_o\).
points: Calcite is a negative crystal.
Away from the optic axis the e-ray is faster: \(v_e > v_o\).
The e-ray is slowest along the optic axis and fastest perpendicular to it.
Principal index: \(\mu_e = c/(v_e)_{\max}\) (Eq. 20.14).

cards.label: 09 · §20.11.3 Definition
cards.title: What is a positive crystal?
cards.body: A positive crystal is a uniaxial crystal in which the e-ray index is greater than the o-ray index, \(\mu_e > \mu_o\).
points: Quartz is a positive crystal.
Away from the optic axis the e-ray is slower: \(v_e < v_o\).
The e-ray is fastest along the optic axis and slowest perpendicular to it.
Principal index: \(\mu_e = c/(v_e)_{\min}\) (Eq. 20.13).

cards.title: Huygens' two wavelets
cards.body: Huygens' explanation gives the o-ray a spherical wavelet and the e-ray an ellipsoidal wavelet inside the crystal.
points: o-wavelet: a sphere; the o-wavefront goes straight ahead.
e-wavelet: an ellipsoid of revolution about the optic axis; speed depends on direction.
The two wave surfaces touch where the optic axis meets them.
The e-wavefront is not perpendicular to its direction of travel.

cards.label: 11 · §20.14 Case 1
cards.title: Optic axis inclined to the refracting edge
cards.body: Light falls normal to the surface, and the o-ray and e-ray leave in different directions with different speeds.
points: The optic axis is inclined to the refracting edge.
The circle (o-wavelet) and ellipse (e-wavelet) touch along the optic axis.
Common tangents KL (o) and EF (e) give the two wavefronts.

cards.label: 12 · §20.14 Case 2(a)
cards.title: Optic axis in plane of incidence, parallel to edge
cards.body: The optic axis lies in the plane of incidence; the o-ray and e-ray travel in the same direction at different speeds.
points: Light falls normal to the face; the optic axis is parallel to edge MN.
The circle and ellipse touch along AM and BN, the optic axis direction.
PR is the o-wavefront (tangent to the circle); QS is the e-wavefront.

cards.label: 13 · §20.14 Case 2(b)
cards.title: Optic axis perpendicular to plane of incidence
cards.body: The optic axis is parallel to edge MN but perpendicular to the plane of incidence; the two rays share a direction.
points: The wavelets touch along a line normal to the plane of incidence.
So the wavelets appear spherical in the plane of incidence.
PR (o) and QS (e) are the common tangents: the two wavefronts.

cards.label: 14 · §20.14 Case 3
cards.title: Optic axis perpendicular to the edge, in plane of incidence
cards.body: The optic axis is perpendicular to edge MN and lies in the plane of incidence.
points: The circle and ellipse touch at P and Q, on the optic axis.
The ellipse minor axis equals the circle radius.
The common tangent PQ is the wavefront for both rays.
The o-ray and e-ray travel in the same direction.

cards.label: Relation · §20.11.2
cards.title: Principal refractive indices
points: \(c\) is the speed of light in vacuum; \(v_o\) is the o-ray speed in the crystal.
Positive crystal: \(\mu_e = c/(v_e)_{\min}\) (Eq. 20.13).
Negative crystal: \(\mu_e = c/(v_e)_{\max}\) (Eq. 20.14).
Negative crystal: \(v_e > v_o\), so \(\mu_o > \mu_e\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Which ray obeys the ordinary laws of refraction?
cards.why: The o-ray has the same speed in every direction, so it follows the ordinary laws. The e-ray does not.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In a negative crystal, which ray is faster away from the optic axis?
cards.why: Negative crystals have \(v_e > v_o\) everywhere except along the optic axis.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: In a ______ crystal the e-wave ellipsoid lies inside the o-wave sphere.
cards.why: Positive crystals have \(\mu_e > \mu_o\), so the e-ellipsoid sits inside the o-sphere.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.why: The book gives \(\mu_o = 1.66\) and \(\mu_e = 1.486\) for calcite.

glossary.definition: A crystal whose refractive index depends on the direction of light travel.
The splitting of one incident ray into an ordinary ray and an extraordinary ray inside an anisotropic crystal.
The crystal direction along which the o-ray and e-ray have the same speed, so no double refraction occurs.
glossary.example: Bisects a blunt corner of calcite

glossary.definition: The plane containing the optic axis and perpendicular to a pair of opposite crystal faces.
glossary.example: Parallelogram with angles 71° and 109° in calcite

glossary.definition: The plane containing the optic axis and either the o-ray or the e-ray.
glossary.example: Sets the vibration direction of each ray

glossary.definition: The refracted ray that obeys the ordinary laws of refraction and has the same speed in every direction.
The refracted ray whose speed and refractive index depend on its direction inside the crystal.
A uniaxial crystal in which the e-ray index is less than the o-ray index, so the o-sphere lies inside the e-ellipsoid.
A uniaxial crystal in which the e-ray index is greater than the o-ray index, so the e-ellipsoid lies inside the o-sphere.
